# Today

## Three Things {.plain-title}

::: {.steps}
1. The data --- twenty-five years of fundamentals and prices, and how to reach it
2. Skills --- how you stop re-explaining yourself to the machine
3. Build one --- a valuation skill that prices a company off its peers
:::

::: {.note}
By the end you will have something in your group's repository that any of you can
point at a ticker.
:::

## The Oldest Valuation Method There Is

::: {.lead}
A company is worth roughly what companies like it are worth.
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
No forecast, no discount rate, no terminal value. Find the peers, take the
middle of their multiples, apply it. It is what a banker does on the back of an
envelope, and it is a real benchmark --- hard to beat and easy to check.
:::

The whole method is three decisions: which multiple, which peers, and what to do
with the ones that do not make sense.

## What Is in There {.plain-title}

| Table | Contents |
|---|---|
| `sep` | Daily open, high, low, close, adjusted close, volume |
| `daily` | Daily valuation ratios and market cap |
| `metrics` | Daily moving averages and other statistics |
| `sf1` | 10-K and 10-Q data, and pre-computed financial ratios |
| `sf2` | Insider trades, from Form 4 |
| `tickers` | Industry, sector, exchange, size category |
| `actions` | Mergers, splits, dividends, ticker changes |
| `events` | SEC 8-K filings and material corporate events |

::: {.note}
A Table Descriptions page on the portal lists every variable in every table.
:::

## Today We Need Three of Them

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[`daily`]{.card-title}

`pe`, `pb`, `ps`, `ev`, `evebit`, `evebitda`, `marketcap` --- one row per stock
per day.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[`tickers`]{.card-title}

`sector`, `industry`, `exchange`, `scalemarketcap`. This is what makes a peer
group a peer group.
:::

::: {.card}
[`sf1`]{.card-title}

The filings. Revenue, earnings, book value, and the ratios computed from them.
:::
:::

## `sf1` Has Dimensions {.band-bottom}

| | Annual | Quarterly | Trailing four quarters |
|---|---|---|---|
| As most recently restated | `MRY` | `MRQ` | `MRT` |
| As originally reported | `ARY` | `ARQ` | `ART` |

::: {.note .note-plum}
Today we use `MRY` --- annual, most recent restatement. It is the cleanest view
of what a company earned. When we start backtesting, we will have to switch,
because `MRY` tells you today what nobody knew at the time.
:::

## Three Things That Trip Everyone {.plain-title}

| | |
|---|---|
| Dates are text | Cast before you compare or sort: `date::DATE`, `reportperiod::DATE` |
| `sf1` has no `date` | Use `reportperiod` for the fiscal period end, `datekey` for the filing date |
| Market cap is in thousands | In `daily`. A $2T company shows up as 2,000,000,000 |

::: {.note}
Each of these produces an answer, not an error. That is what makes them
expensive.
:::

# Pulling It

## Start by Looking Around

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Using the data portal, show me the columns in `daily` and `tickers`, and give
> me five rows of each.

::: {.note}
Before any analysis, look at the actual rows. Half of the mistakes in this
course get caught here, in thirty seconds, by someone who looked.
:::

## The Pull {.band-bottom}

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> For the most recent date in `daily`, get `ticker`, `pe`, and `marketcap` for
> every stock. Join `sector` and `industry` from `tickers`. Then pull the `MRY`
> rows from `sf1` for the most recent fiscal year and bring in revenue, net
> income, and shares outstanding. Show me the SQL before you run it.

::: {.note .note-plum}
That last sentence is the entire lesson from Tuesday, in six words.
:::

## Read the SQL {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
You are not checking whether it is elegant. You are checking four things.
:::

| | |
|---|---|
| Did it filter the dimension? | Without `dimension = 'MRY'` you get six rows per company-year |
| Did it cast the dates? | Text comparison on dates goes wrong quietly |
| Is the join key right? | `ticker` is not unique across time --- see `actions` |
| How many rows came back? | You know roughly how many listed stocks there are |

## What a P/E of --12 Means

::: {.lead}
Nothing. It means the company lost money.
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
A negative P/E is not a cheap stock. It is a stock with no E. Left in the sample
it drags the median in the wrong direction and makes the cheapest-looking
companies the ones that are losing the most.
:::

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Drop the negative P/E rows, and show me how many you dropped by sector.

## Look Before You Compute {.plain-title}

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Histogram of P/E across all stocks. Then the same by sector, and a table of
> the count, median, and the 10th and 90th percentiles in each.

::: {.note}
You are looking for two things: how fat the right tail is, and whether the
sectors actually differ. If they do not, the peer group is doing no work and the
method has nothing to offer.
:::

# Median of Peers

## Why the Median {.compare}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[The mean]{.eyebrow}

One company with a P/E of 900 --- a real company that barely broke even --- and
the average for the industry is meaningless.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[The median]{.eyebrow}

Unmoved by the tail. With ratios, where the numerator is bounded below and the
denominator can approach zero, this is not a refinement. It is the difference
between a number and noise.
:::
::::

## Which Peers? {.band-bottom}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[Sector]{.card-title}

Eleven of them. Always enough companies, often not comparable ones.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Industry]{.card-title}

Much finer. Sometimes four companies, and then the median is one company's P/E.
:::

::: {.card}
[Industry and size]{.card-title}

Better in principle. Cuts the group again, so you need to watch the count.
:::
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
There is no correct answer. There is a choice you make, write down, and defend
when you present.
:::

## The Calculation

::: {.steps}
1. Group the stocks by peer set, and drop the ones with no meaningful P/E
2. Take the median P/E in each group
3. Multiply it by the company's own earnings per share
4. Compare with the price it actually trades at
:::

::: {.note}
The gap is the whole output. A company trading well below its peer median is
either cheap or different, and the method cannot tell you which.
:::

## Now Do It {.plain-title}

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Compute the median P/E within each industry. For every stock, report its own
> P/E, its industry median, and the ratio of the two. Show me the twenty most
> expensive and the twenty cheapest by that ratio.

::: {.note}
Read the two lists. If the cheap list is all one industry, or all tiny
companies, something in the peer definition is doing work you did not intend.
:::

# Skills

## Stop Re-Explaining Yourself

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[Always on]{.card-title}

Applies to every conversation you have.

Who you are, how you want to be written to, what never to do.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Per project]{.card-title}

Applies inside one folder.

This course, this dataset, its quirks.
:::

::: {.card}
[When relevant]{.card-title}

A skill: read only when what you asked matches what it is for.
:::
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
Three scopes, and the third is the interesting one --- because it costs nothing
until it applies.
:::

## A Skill Is Written Instructions, Filed Where They Can Be Found

A folder with a `SKILL.md` in it. Two parts: a line saying when to use it, and
the instructions for how.

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[At startup]{.card-title}

It reads only the name and the one-line description --- a few dozen words per skill.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[When it matches]{.card-title}

Only then does it open the file and read the rest.
:::

::: {.card}
[Which is why you can have many]{.card-title}

A hundred installed skills cost nothing until one of them is relevant.
:::
:::

::: {.note}
Not a plugin, and not code. A written procedure.
:::

## `CLAUDE.md` Versus a Skill {.compare}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[`CLAUDE.md` --- always read]{.eyebrow}

What is always true here: what the project is, where things live, the
conventions, what never to do.

Read at the start of every session in that folder.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[A skill --- read when relevant]{.eyebrow}

A procedure for a particular kind of job.

Standing facts go in `CLAUDE.md`. Procedures go in skills.
:::
::::

::: {.note}
Ask GLM to write the first `CLAUDE.md` for you --- it will read the folder and draft it.
:::

## Why This Matters to a Group {.band-bottom}

::: {.lead}
The skill is a file. The file is in the repository.
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
Which means the decision is made once, by one of you, and the other two get it
by pulling. It also means the decision is visible: when you present, the skill
is the record of what you chose and why.
:::

Every ad-hoc instruction typed into a prompt window dies with that conversation.

# Build One

## Get It Right Once, Then Save It

::: {.steps}
1. Get the peer-median valuation working the way you want it, in a conversation
2. Say: save that as a skill
3. Start a fresh session and ask it to value a different company
:::

::: {.note}
Step 3 is the test. If it needs to be told anything you already decided, the
skill is not finished.
:::

## What Has to Be Written Down {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[The decisions]{.card-title}

Which multiple. Which peer definition. Median, not mean. What the minimum group
size is.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[The traps]{.card-title}

`dimension = 'MRY'`. Cast the dates. Market cap is in thousands. Drop negative
earnings.
:::

::: {.card}
[The output]{.card-title}

What it should hand back every time: the peer set and its size, the median, the
implied value, the gap.
:::
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
The middle card is the one that pays for itself. Those four traps will otherwise
bite each of you, separately, for six weeks.
:::

## Exercise

::: {.steps}
1. Build the skill in your group's repository
2. Test it on a company none of you used while building it
3. Then test it on a bank, and on a company that lost money last year
4. Commit and push it
:::

::: {.note}
Steps 2 and 3 are where you find out what you left implicit. Write down what
broke --- it is what you will present on Tuesday.
:::

## Where It Will Fail {.band-bottom}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[The industry of one]{.card-title}

A peer group with three companies in it has a median that is one company's opinion.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Financials]{.card-title}

P/E means something different for a bank. So does book value.
:::

::: {.card}
[Growth]{.card-title}

Two companies in the same industry with different growth rates should not trade
at the same multiple. The method assumes they do.
:::
:::

::: {.note}
The third one is what Thursday of next week is about: predicting the multiple
instead of borrowing it.
:::

::: {.steps}
1. Finish the skill, and push it
2. Run it on five companies you know something about, and see whether the answers are sane
